newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Jiang vows to pursue Deng Xiaoping reforms.
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang vows to pursue Deng Xiaoping reforms.

text.p: Deng Xiaoping's heir President Jiang Zemin fought back tears on Tuesday as he eulogised the late strongman and said the future lay in the capitalist-style reforms of the revolutionary who transformed China.

As final rites began for Deng, who died last Wednesday aged 92, sirens and whistles wailed nationwide for three minutes to lament the man who delivered unprecedented prosperity to the world's most populous nation while keeping communists in charge.

In Beijing's cavernous Great Hall of the People, 10,000 of China's elite Mao-suited revolutionaries mingled with Western- suited technocrats to bow before Deng's ashes. Missing was Deng's close comrade, hardliner Peng Zhen, who was ill.
They heard Jiang, Deng's protege and now China's most powerful man, sob theatrically at the start of a 50-minute eulogy.
"The people of China love Comrade Deng Xiaoping, thank Comrade Deng Xiaoping, mourn for Comrade Deng Xiaoping, and cherish the memory of Comrade Deng Xiaoping," Jiang said.

In a simple ceremony in line with Deng's wishes, Jiang reaffirmed Deng's distinctive formula of economic reform mixed with socialism, saying: "Reform is the inevitable road through which China will be able to achieve socialist modernisation."

On the stage beneath a black-framed portrait of a smiling, avuncular Deng lay a casket containing his ashes, draped with a red hammer-and-sickle communist flag and surrounded by flowers and a wreath from his grieving family. His ashes are to be scattered at sea.

But in hosannas to the lifelong communist who forged a fledgling economic superpower out of a Stalinist backwater, Jiang glossed over what many see as Deng's darkest hour -- his 1989 use of the army to crush pro-democracy protests centred on Tiananmen Square. "We withstood the severe test," Jiang said.
On Tuesday, in the vast square adjoining the Great Hall, Beijing's authoritarian hand was in evidence.
Police cleared the square after dawn, throwing a security net over an arena that is a potent symbol of China and a focus for expressions of grief as well as demonstrations of anger.
One small group of people who unfurled a banner of mourning were quickly asked to leave and police ushered away a weeping elderly couple who tried to lay a wreath.

On the Beijing Commodity Exchange, traders shut down their computer terminals and stood with heads bowed out of respect to Deng, who introduced all manner of capitalist-style innovations, from stocks and bonds to pawn shops and night clubs.

Jiang seized upon the eulogy and emotional displays for the deceased patriarch to remind pretenders to his throne, and the 1.2 billion people over whom he now holds sway, that he is in charge, diplomats said.
"Under the party's leadership with Jiang Zemin as its core, carry out the unfulfilled wishes of Deng Xiaoping," read a banner hanging from a balcony in the Great Hall.
Jiang issued his strongest pledge yet to recover the island of Taiwan, an achievement that had eluded both Deng and Mao.
"The Taiwan question will be settled eventually and the complete reunification of the motherland will certainly be achieved," Jiang promised.

The man who holds China's top three jobs -- party chief, state president and commander-in-chief of the armed forces -- assured the three-million-strong People's Liberation Army that they would not be forgotten as China races to modernise.
Analysts say the support of the military is essential for Jiang's survival as he emerges from seven years under the wing of his powerful patron.
On Monday, television showed China's millions indelible final images of their dead leader lying in state, his face a puffy deathmask. It was the first glimpse of their ruler in three years.
It was the sort of lingering display of his remains that Deng -- contemptuous of the personality cult around his predecessor Mao Zedong -- had forbidden.
"Deng looked at peace," the Xinhua news agency said.
Political analysts questioned, however, whether the patriarch would have been at ease with the way his successors have handled the delicate transition period.
